headlines.title: Traffic alerts: I-80 Carquinez Bridge closure, limited Highway 101 access in SF
headlines.description: Construction projects on both sides of the Bay this weekend are expected to cause delays for motorists. Here’s what to know about the projects and how to plan ahead. Westbound Carquinez Bridge on Interstate 80 to shut down Caltrans will close the westbound Carquinez Bridge on Interstate 80 for 53 hours starting Friday night as crews work on a deck rehabilitation project. The closure will start at 10 p.m. and continue through the weekend. It is scheduled to end by 3 a.m. Monday. The eastbound direction of the bridge will remain open. The San Francisco Bay Ferry said it would provide additional ferry trips Saturday and Sunday on the Vallejo route during the westbound closure. The exact closure will be westbound I-80 between the east end of the bridge and start of the westbound off-ramp to Pomona Street, from Sonoma Boulevard, Sequoia Avenue, Magazine Street and Lincoln Road. Below is a map of the closure: Detours during weekend Carquinez Bridge closure Motorists traveling westbound from Sacramento can take the following alternate routes: Detour for westbound I-80 traffic (before Exit 4): Take exit 40 to merge onto southbound Interstate 680 Continue on southbound I-680 Take exit 53 to merge onto westbound Highway 4 Continue on westbound Highway 4 Take exit 1B, merge onto westbound I-80 To completely avoid the Carquinez Bridge closure, motorists can use westbound I-680. Regional detour map for motorists traveling westbound from Sacramento (Caltrans) Detour for southbound Highway 29 traffic: Detour to Curtola Parkway and stay in the through lane at the Curtola Parkway/Lemon Street intersection to merge onto eastbound Interstate 780 Continue on eastbound I-780 and stay in the left lane Take exit 7B to merge onto southbound I-680 Continue on southbound I-680 Take exit 53 to merge onto westbound I-80 Detour for South Vallejo/Carquinez Heights traffic: Detour to northbound Highway 29 (Sonoma Boulevard) Make a right turn onto Lemon Street Continue on Lemon Street and make a right turn at Curtola Parkway/Lemon Street to merge onto eastbound I-780 Continue on eastbound I-780 and stay in the left lane Take exit 7B to merge onto southbound I-680 Continue on southbound I-680 Take exit 53 to merge onto westbound Hwy. 4 Continue on westbound Hwy. 4 Take exit 1B to merge onto westbound I-80 Local detour map for motorists traveling westbound from Sacramento (Caltrans) Limited Highway 101 access in San Francisco Starting Friday at 11 p.m., Caltrans will close two lanes in each direction of the Highway 101 Bayshore Freeway (Hospital Curve) area in San Francisco and expects to keep them closed until 6 a.m. Monday. The impacted portion of Highway 101 will be between Cesar Chavez and 17th streets so Caltrans can work on Hospital Curve rehabilitation, which is part of a longer-term project that started in 2025. Another closure is planned for Sept. 4-7. How to avoid Highway 101 traffic Caltrans is suggesting Interstate 280 or public transportation as an option as they shutter the lanes to work on the median near Hospital Curve. Bay City News contributed to this report. San Francisco Aug 20 Transportation Jul 20

headlines.title: New York passes San Francisco as top tech market
headlines.description: New numbers show the job market is growing in the South Bay even as New York has taken a bigger bite out of the Bay Area’s tech workforce. Commercial real estate firm Cboe Global Markets says for the first time ever, New York City has surpassed San Francisco in total tech jobs. Those tech jobs gave the Bay Area a boost in the latest state jobs report. It shows the artificial intelligence boom is largely responsible for the South Bay adding thousands of new jobs in July, even as California overall lost 20,000 jobs. Scott Budman examines the latest figures in his video report above.

headlines.title: Auction features work of legendary Bay Area photographer Michael Zagaris
headlines.description: From Friday through Sunday, work from legendary Bay Area photographer Michael Zagaris will be up for sale through Heritage Auctions. Zagaris has covered some of the biggest events in Bay Area sports and music history. The work for sale includes photographs of Joe Montana and Bill Walsh, along with jerseys from Montana, John Taylor, Ronnie Lott, and Dwight Clark. The collection also spans his work with the A’s, the Rolling Stones and The Who. Raj Mathai talked to Zagaris about the auction. Watch the full interview in the video above.

headlines.title: Palo Alto prepares to audit Flock camera system amid questions over data access
headlines.description: Another Bay Area city is set to wade into the growing controversy over Flock Safety cameras. Palo Alto said it’s preparing to audit its Flock camera system after learning data had been shared through a nationwide network despite local policies limiting who could access it. Law enforcement officials say the automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are critical to public safety, but critics argue they are a dangerous invasion of privacy and are abused by law enforcement. Palo Alto’s independent police auditor, the OIR Group, is expected to review the city’s rules around data sharing, outside access and data retention, as well as how the camera technology is being used. “Our audit is really intended to ensure that if there is misuse, that misuse is immediately identified through internal audits, through other guardrails, training, limitations as to who gets access to the information,” said Michael Gennaco with the OIR Group. The Palo Alto City Council is expected to finalize the scope of the independent audit Monday before deciding what, if anything, should change about the city’s use of the cameras. Brentwood Aug 17 Technology Aug 13 East Bay Jul 31 The audit comes as a handful of other Bay Area communities rethink their relationship with Flock. Some cities have ended their contracts altogether, while others have decided to scale back use. In a statement, Palo Alto’s police chief said the cameras have provided a significant public safety benefit. “ALPR has been a tremendous investigative tool,” the statement read. “It has helped us solve cases, recover stolen vehicles and property, apprehend wanted individuals, and safely locate missing and suicidal persons. I am confident that our officers are using the technology responsibly and to good effect.” Critics of the cameras disagree. “We want to make sure that value isn’t overridden by the lack of trust in misuse of the data,” Gennaco said. In addressing some of the concerns surrounding how the data is used, Flock Safety CEO Garrett Langley said, “We don’t own the data. Our customers do. We don’t work with ICE. The customer chooses whom to share that data with. So I’ve found that once people see the truth, they go, ‘This feels like a very good trade-off. But at the end of the day, we have to find a society where safety and privacy can coexist.” Langley said he also supports regulation, including rules around data retention and accountability. “We give power to those who are entitled and ask them to keep us safe, and the accountability has to come with that,” he said. “When I look at regulation, I say there are a couple of things we have to get right. we have to decide how long this data should live, whether it’s seven days, 30 days or a year.”

headlines.title: Bay Area man's proposal aims to remove taxes on restaurant meals
headlines.description: A Bay Area man is proposing eliminating taxes on restaurant meals and wants voters to weigh in if the legislature does not act. If passed, the proposal would mean cities and the state would lose valuable tax revenue. Damian Trujillo takes a closer look. Watch his report in the video above.

headlines.title: ‘So rewarding': Sunnyvale woman hopes her animal adoption adventure inspires others
headlines.description: Diane Foxen’s Sunnyvale home is not just filled with animals, it’s filled with love. The ICU nurse is extra busy these days nursing tuxedo kittens back to health. “It is so rewarding to take care of them, to see them go from this little sick kitten or small kitten that doesn’t know how to eat yet to this big, feisty, running around these guys, playing, loving, purring, and ready for their next adventure in life so that you can start your next adventure,” Foxen said. Foxen’s own adventure started when her son grew up and moved away. She said she became depressed due to empty nest syndrome and the COVID-19 lockdown. But then a cat named Orion filled that empty space. “Orion was one of those foster kittens,” Foxen said. “He was super, super sick, and he just showed his resilience and the will to survive and showed me how precious life is.” The bond convinced Foxen to be even more adventurous. She and Orion completed a 900-mile bike-a-thon from Canada to California to raise money for Humane Society Silicon Valley. “He was my little tent partner,” Foxen said. “He was my camping partner. That bond just kind of filled that empty space, gave back to me what I gave back to him.” Foxen said she hopes her story inspires people to take part in the Clear The Shelters animal adoption campaign and shows that adoption is a journey taken one step at a time. Community Aug 3 clear the shelters Aug 14 “If you’re on the fence about adopting, foster first,” she said. “It’s a great way to see, ‘Will this fit into my lifestyle?'” Max Piekarus with Humane Society Silicon Valley said fostering helps more animals get adopted. “Oftentimes you’ll have someone foster and fall in love, like Diane did with Orion, and adopt, which is always a great outcome, but ideally one person will foster until they’re ready for adoption.” Foxen pointed out that love requires responsibility, like making sure pets are spayed or neutered so they don’t add to the population of homeless animals. Then, enjoy the adventure. “Don’t be afraid to try to foster and to adopt and make space for those animals that are helpless and looking for someone to love them,” she said.

headlines.title: Farmers hope new steam technology will eliminate use of pesticides
headlines.description: Farmworkers have claimed for years that contact with pesticides has left them battling cancer, neurological disorders and other ailments. A new technology aims to weed out pesticides by turning to steam. National advocacy group Farmworker Justice has been fighting the use of toxic pesticides on crops for years. The Environmental Protection Agency estimates that roughly 10,000 to 20,000 farmworkers suffer from acute pesticide poisonings every year. Shinta Kawahara Family Farms in Santa Cruz County believes it has found a better way. The organic farm is testing new technology that uses high pressure steam, instead of toxic fumigants, to prep the soil before a plant or seed goes into the ground. Rod Koda’s farm was one of the first in the nation to begin testing the steam technology, and he believes it’s working. “I don’t have the plant mortality, and the fruit would be bigger because the plant is not stressed, the root is not stressed,” Koda said. Researchers say the steam serves as a herbicide and reduces plant disease by 70%, killing the soil pests. The strawberry commission is on board, as is David Sanford, the agriculture commissioner in Santa Cruz County. “It’s early on in their field trials, but the work that we’ve seen so far is pretty promising and it shows a lot of potential,” Sanford said. “It needs research. It needs work.” The hope is to one day limit or eliminate the need for pesticides on crops. “This is the first season and it’s really exciting,” Koda said.

headlines.title: Backcountry guide company faces $150K in fines after California's deadliest modern avalanche
headlines.description: California workplace safety officials have fined a guide company that was leading backcountry skiers down a mountain in February when an avalanche was triggered, killing nine members of the group in the deadliest avalanche in the state’s modern history. The California Division of Occupational Safety and Health, or Cal/OSHA, issued $151,300 in fines against Blackbird Mountain Guides for seven alleged violations it found. The largest fine, $81,000, was for “failing to correct the imminent hazard posed by traveling in avalanche terrain when the avalanche danger was rated high.” The agency issued the fines earlier this month. Blackbird Mountain Guides said it has filed a formal appeal and that it believes it was in “full compliance” with all regulatory requirements. A separate investigation by Cal/OSHA’s Bureau of Investigations, which reviews workplace deaths for possible criminal charges, is ongoing, the agency said in a Friday statement. The Nevada County Sheriff’s Department has forwarded results of its own criminal investigation to the district attorney’s office for review of possible criminal charges, said Ashley Quadros, a spokesperson with the sheriff’s office. The DA’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The nine people who died were part of a group of 15 backcountry skiers headed out on a three-day trek organized by Blackbird Mountain Guides into pristine wilderness near Frog Lake in California’s Sierra Nevada as a powerful winter stormmoved into the state. Three of the dead were guides. Northern California Aug 9 Sierra Nevada Apr 6 California Apr 2 The skiers made their way to remote huts located at 7,600 feet (2,316 meters) in Tahoe National Forest, carrying their own food and supplies. Two days later, on Feb. 17, the group was attempting to ski down the mountain when an avalanche hit near Castle Peak, trapping them. Six skiers, including one guide, were rescued after sheltering in place for hours as searchers battled blizzard conditions to reach them. Cal/OSHA, which issued the fines on Aug. 12, found the company allegedly failed “to correct the imminent hazard posed by traveling in avalanche terrain when the avalanche danger was rated high.” The other five violations are related to alleged workplace violations, including not providing employees with effective training and failing to report the three employees’ deaths to the agency in a timely manner. “The citations do not reflect the reality of our profession or the safety program we have built,” Blackbird Mountain Guides said in a statement. “Mountain guiding takes place in dynamic wilderness environments where conditions change minute to minute — it’s not a controlled setting such as construction sites. We welcome the opportunity to work with Cal/OSHA to contextualize the unique realities of operating in backcountry environments.” The guides on the trip had years of experience in backcountry skiing and certifications from the American Mountain Guides Association, which offers the highest level of training in the industry, the company said. “Guides pursue knowledge and excellence as a lifelong responsibility and the guides on this trip approached their work with care and professionalism,” said Blackbird Mountain Guides owner Zeb Blais.
headlines.source: Olga R. Rodriguez | The Associated Press

headlines.title: Man dies after shooting at a home in Fremont
headlines.description: A man died following a shooting at a home in Fremont Friday, according to the police department. Police said they received reports of a shooting at a home on San Pedro Drive at around 12:13 p.m. At the scene, responding officers found a man suffering from a gunshot wound, according to officials. Authorities said the man was given medical assistance and taken to a local trauma center, where he died. Police said preliminary investigation indicates a group of men was at the scene when the shooting occurred. The police department said some people who were trying to run away from the scene were taken into custody. Authorities said the case remains under investigation and do not believe there are any outstanding suspects or threats to public safety. They added this is the city’s third homicide of 2026. The police department asks anyone with information to contact their Investigations Unit at 510-790-6900. headlines.title: 2 injured in Pittsburg house fire
headlines.description: Two people were injured in a Pittsburg house fire Friday morning, with one person taken to a hospital with second- and third-degree burns. Contra Costa County Fire Protection District crews were sent to the home at 69 Atherton Ave. at about 11:40 a.m. and were able to knock down the single-alarm blaze by about 11:45 a.m., according to Fire Capt. Victor Daniel. One person was treated at the scene for smoke inhalation and one person suffered burns that required hospitalization, Daniel said. Fire officials announced at a little after noon that the fire was extinguished, but crews were still at the scene and people are being asked to stay away from the area. The cause of the fire is still under investigation.

headlines.title: California officials warn against invasive species
headlines.description: If not managed properly, invasive species in California could further harm local ecology, damage infrastructure and impact economic activity, state officials and experts said during a virtual briefing Thursday. The golden mussel and the glassy-winged sharpshooter were among invasive species discussed in the briefing by representatives from the California Natural Resources Agency, Department of Water Resources, Department of Food and Agriculture, and the Department of Pesticide Regulation. Golden mussels are an invasive freshwater species of mussel, originally from Southeast Asia. The species was first detected in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta in October 2024, and authorities do not know how they arrived in California, said Kristopher Jones, an assistant manager at the California Department of Water Resources. Since then, Jones said, the mussels have spread to water bodies all over the state. “They’re moving pretty quickly since they were detected,” he said. “They’re becoming an infrastructure and water supply issue.” In April, the San Joaquin County Board of Supervisors proclaimed a local emergency because of golden mussels and their impacts on the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta. Jones explained that the mussels proliferate fast, competing with native species of aquatic life, and attach to hard surfaces like the bottom of boats, pipes and other water infrastructure. As a result, they can clog waterways and damage vital water infrastructure. Jones said that the Department of Water Resources and the Department of Fish and Wildlife are working to use different treatment methods. To avoid inadvertently spreading the golden mussels, Jones urged watercraft users, “before you move your boat from one water body to another, clean it, drain it completely and let it dry.” Another invasive pest is threatening California’s winegrape industry — the glassy-winged sharpshooter. The glassy-winged sharpshooter is a leafhopper insect and spreads the fatal grapevine ailment known as Pierce’s disease, a bacterial infection that blocks water-conducting systems in plants, causing them to dry out. The disease is incurable. In May, the California Department of Food and Agriculture found that grapevines infested with the insect were supplied to multiple Costco locations across California. The plants, numbering in the thousands, came from Burchell Nursery in Fresno County. Since then, the California Department of Food and Agriculture and county agricultural officials have been tracking the pest, setting up traps, and destroying infested grapevines to prevent further spread. A 2025 study funded in part by the Pierce’s Disease/Glassy-Winged Sharpshooter Board at the California Department of Food and Agriculture estimated that if the pest is allowed to spread unchecked, it could cost the state’s winegrape growers an additional $56 million a year in lost production and vine replacement. The pest already costs growers roughly $48 million in lost winegrape production and vine replacement every year, the study added. Attacking the pest early on is the best shot at controlling its spread, as small and isolated populations are easier to tackle, said Jeff Dukes, senior staff scientist at the Carnegie Institution for Science. A winegrape industry group has committed $820,000 to the effort, and the CDFA estimates that it spent $3.2 million in its initial response in May and June. “When you spend money on catching new invaders early, that can make a big difference because you can get rid of the invading population,” Dukes said.

headlines.title: Protesters who shut down the Golden Gate Bridge in 2024 sentenced
headlines.description: Seven protesters who were convicted of blocking the Golden Gate Bridge at the start of the Israel-Hamas war were sentenced by a San Francisco judge Friday. Six were convicted of multiple misdemeanors, including false imprisonment, in connection with the 2024 protest. They each got six months of probation, 30 days in jail (15 of those can be served while on work release), and a $1,000 fine. Prosecutors argued bystanders who were trapped on the bridge by the protest for hours were being held against their will. A seventh protestor was also convicted of failing to disburse. Back in 2024, protesters shut down the Golden Gate Bridge for hours during the morning commute. The protesters, dubbed the “Golden Gate 26,” were eventually arrested and hit with multiple charges, including false imprisonment. As the judge was imposing her sentence protester supporters were again making their case that this was an act of free speech, not a crime. “My comrades are deeply principled people. And they are very brave people. And I know that when they are in that jail, they will be sharing that commissary. They will be educating others. They will be caring for other incarcerated people. But knowing that they have to spend even another night, after we already spent four days in that jail, is horrifying,” protest supporter Jordan Harger said. During the sentencing, the judge referenced Martin Luther King Jr., who during the Civil Rights Movement wrote about accepting a sentence as part of the consequences of a just protest. The judge also said the Golden Gate Bridge protestors only ended their demonstration when their personal property was threatened; they had chained themselves together while sitting in their cars as they were blocking traffic. According to the judge, the CHP told them they would need to sew vehicles apart in order to separate them. The majority of the protesters avoided trial, but seven of them went through a weekslong trial that ended with a guilty verdict for false imprisonment. The protesters narrowly avoided a more severe charge of felony conspiracy, which could have carried a maximum sentence of 15 years in prison. Each person also spent four days in jail when they were first arrested so they will get credit for time served and they were granted bail as they appeal this sentence so they can stay out of jail during that process. The District Attorney’s Office also decided not to seek a retrial for the felony charge of conspiracy, saying that would not be in the best interest of justice. San Francisco Jul 2 San Francisco May 20 Protesters face trial over Golden Gate Bridge shutdown
headlines.source: Ginger Conejero Saab and Sergio Quintana
